doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Captain Buckles: Dorn does not recognise his own Fathead Newman record
summary: Monk Rowe plays Fathead Newman tracks Dorn produced and Dorn cannot place them. He tells how the album title Captain Buckles came from Fathead's raincoat.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Let me drop the needle for you. Okay?
Go baby. Is it going to be something I did that I’ll forget that I did, which is another one of my great traits?
[audio interlude]
Did I make that record?
Yes you did. As a matter of fact I think —
I don’t even know who it is.
Okay well, let me find the —
Would that be Yusef or Rahsaan or something?
No, this is the same guy that, this might —
You understand that I barely — I didn’t make that record.
Yes you did. That’s Fathead.
Maybe my brother made that.
Well your name was on the record. In fact, that first piece I played for you —
“Little Sister?”
That first piece I played for you was called “Joel’s — oh I lost my page.
“Joel’s Lament?” Joel’s something. Oh you know what? Is that with Blue Mitchell? Fathead and Blue Mitchell?
It was called “Joel’s Domain.”
“Joel’s Domain,” right.
Yeah. Bernard Purdie on drums.
Man. Once again I put the all the R&B guys in there.
Yeah.
People — critics used to hate that stuff man. That sounded good. I made that?
Yeah, you made that record.
Do you know the name of the album?
Yeah, “Captain —
“Captain Buckles.”
Yeah.

That’s with Blue Mitchell. I loved that. Now this is imbecilic. I loved that record but I didn’t recognize that record. Yeah that was a great little record, “Captain” — and you know where we got the title from that? Fathead came in, right? And it was like I don’t know maybe middle of winter or end of winter, or something in there, and it was chilly outside and it was raining. And he had a brand new raincoat. And you know, like really stylish, with all kinds of buckles and bells and whistles and buttons and epaulets and flaps and all this kind of stuff. And he walked in and Blue was there and he looked at him and he said, “ahhh, Captain Buckles.” So I said to Fats, I said, “we got the title for the album, now let’s get the music.” And I think I had Zagorski, Stanislaw Zagorski who had done all those great illustrations on the Atlantic Records, I think he did a painting of David with a raincoat full ‘o buckles. That’s wild. That sounded good. It sounded better than what I remember doing you know.
I love that when you’ve done so much work that —

You know when you say that to people, you say I don’t remember, I don’t remember it, and they say like oh yeah sure, you don’t remember it. I don’t remember it. Now I’m going to go home and listen to that record if I can find it.
Well it was good.
“Captain Buckles.”
That would have been, oh, mid-sixties. No, no, ’72 I think it was.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. “Captain Buckles.”
